message.content:
In Texas, tenants have several statutory protections and responsibilities under the Texas Property Code and related laws. Below is an overview of key rights you typically enjoy as a renter: | Category | Typical Tenant Rights (Texas) | Notes | |----------|------------------------------|-------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlords may charge up to one month’s rent for a furnished unit and two months’ rent for an unfurnished unit.
• Must be returned within 30 days after lease ends, minus deductions for damages beyond normal wear & tear. | Landlord must provide a written itemized list of deductions if any. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must maintain the premises in a safe, sanitary condition; this includes functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, and structural integrity.
• Must comply with local health and building codes. | If landlord fails, tenants may withhold rent, repair & deduct, or terminate the lease. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • Landlord cannot enter without proper notice (usually 24‑hour written notice unless emergency).
• Landlord must respect your right to privacy. | Exceptions: emergencies, repairs, inspections with notice, or if lease allows otherwise. | | **Notice Requirements** | • For non‑payment of rent: 3‑day notice to pay or vacate.
• For lease termination: 30‑day notice for month‑to‑month agreements; 60‑day notice for longer leases. | Notice must be in writing and delivered personally or via certified mail. | | **Repair & Deduct** | • If landlord fails to fix major problems, tenant may repair and deduct cost from rent (up to $500). | Must give landlord written notice and keep receipts. | | **Rent Control** | • Texas has no statewide rent control; rent increases are governed by lease terms and local ordinances. | Some cities may have local ordinances limiting increases. | | **Discrimination Protections** | • Protected classes: race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, etc. | Under federal Fair Housing Act and Texas Fair Housing Act. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must serve a valid notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for non‑payment).
• Eviction must go through court; unlawful eviction (self‑help) is prohibited. | Tenants can contest eviction in court. | | **Lease Terms** | • Lease must be in writing for >1 year; must include rent amount, security deposit, lease term, and contact info. | Oral leases are enforceable but harder to prove. | | **Utilities** | • Landlord must provide hot water, electricity, gas, and water unless otherwise specified. | Lease may specify which utilities tenant pays. | | **Subletting / Assignment** | • Tenant may sublet only with landlord’s consent (unless lease prohibits). | Landlord cannot unreasonably deny consent. | | **Maintenance Responsibilities** | • Tenant must keep premises clean and report needed repairs promptly. | Failure to report can affect landlord’s ability to claim damages. | ### Practical Steps If You Face Issues 1. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of lease, notices, emails, photos of damage, and repair receipts. 2. **Written Notice** – Send any complaints or requests for repairs in writing (email or certified mail). 3. **Know Your Local Ordinances** – Some cities (e.g., Austin, Dallas) have additional tenant protections. 4. **Seek Legal Aid** – If disputes arise, consider contacting a local tenant advocacy group or legal aid organization. If you need a specific document—like a lease agreement or a notice of intent to terminate—you can let me know, and I can help draft it.
